title: SSCP (2025 outline) practice exam
note: Original questions written for MyNextCert from ISC2's public SSCP exam outline (effective Oct 1, 2025). Not real exam questions. The real SSCP is adaptive (100-125 items, multiple choice and advanced item types); this is a fixed 100-item stand-in with 3 advanced items.

q.q: Your manager tells you to skip the vulnerability scan on a customer-facing server so a release can ship on time, and to mark the scan as done. Under the ISC2 Code of Ethics, what should you do?
o: Refuse to fake the record and raise the risk properly
Right. Acting honorably and honestly comes before serving your principal, and falsifying a record breaks both.
Mark it done, because your duty to your employer comes first
Duty to principals is the third canon. Honesty and protecting the public come before it.
Run the scan secretly overnight without telling anyone, then mark it done
Hiding work from your manager isn't honest either. Raise it openly.
Report the manager to the police
Skipping a scan isn't a crime. Use internal channels first.

q.q: Your company's code of conduct lets employees accept small gifts from vendors, but you're evaluating that vendor's bid right now. What is the BEST action?
o: Decline the gift while the evaluation is open
Right. Even an allowed gift creates a conflict of interest during a decision you influence.
Accept it, because the code allows small gifts
Allowed in general doesn't mean appropriate while you're judging the vendor.
Accept it and give the vendor a slightly better score to be fair
That's exactly the bias a conflict of interest creates.
Accept it and tell the other bidders about it
Telling competitors doesn't remove the conflict.

q.q: A peer on another team asks you to share a client's penetration test report so he can "learn the format." The report has the client's open vulnerabilities. What should you do?
o: Offer a blank template instead
Right. You help a colleague (advancing the profession) without exposing a client's confidential findings.
Send it, since he works for the same company
Being a coworker doesn't give him a need to know this client's weaknesses.
Send it after deleting the client's name and logo
The vulnerabilities and network details can still identify the client and help an attacker.
Ignore his request completely
You can still help him without sharing confidential data.

q.q: An admin uses a shared "admin" account to change firewall rules, and a bad change takes down the VPN. Which principle does the shared account MOST directly break?
o: Accountability
Right. With a shared login, the logs can't show which person made the change.
Availability
The outage hurt availability, but the shared account breaks accountability.
Confidentiality
No data was exposed.
Defense in depth
Defense in depth is about layering controls, not tying actions to people.

q.q: A database stores a hash of each record, and a nightly job recalculates the hashes and alerts on any mismatch. Which security goal does this support?
o: Integrity
Right. A changed hash shows the record was altered.
Confidentiality
Hashes don't hide the record from anyone who can read the database.
Availability
Checking hashes doesn't keep the database up.
Non-repudiation
A plain hash doesn't prove who made a change. That needs a signature tied to a person.

q.q: A hospital lets nurses see only the records of patients on their own ward, even though the system holds every patient's file. Which concept is this?
o: Need to know
Right. Access is limited to the information each person's duties require.
Separation of duties
SoD splits steps of a process between people.
Non-repudiation
Non-repudiation proves who performed an action.
Mandatory vacation
Mandatory vacation helps uncover fraud by rotating people out.

q.q: An auditor asks how the company knows its rule that admin accounts must use MFA is actually followed. Which evidence is BEST?
o: An identity system report of each admin's MFA status
Right. System-generated evidence shows the control is in place for every account.
The written MFA policy signed by the CISO
A policy shows intent, not that it's being followed.
An email from the lead admin confirming that every admin uses MFA
A statement from one person isn't evidence.
The MFA vendor's marketing brochure
A brochure says what the product can do, not how it's configured.

q.q: A company must meet a regulation that requires encrypting cardholder data. It enables database encryption and runs a quarterly check that confirms it's on. What is the quarterly check?
o: A compliance verification of the control
Right. It confirms the control is still working and meets the requirement.
A compensating control
A compensating control replaces one that can't be used.
A deterrent control
A check doesn't discourage attackers.
A risk acceptance
Nothing here accepts risk. The control is in place and verified.

q.q: A small office can't afford a separate security team. Which control gives the MOST risk reduction for the cost against ransomware?
o: Offline, tested backups
Right. With good backups, ransomware can't hold the data hostage, so the business can recover.
A larger internet connection
Bandwidth doesn't protect against ransomware.
A second monitor for every employee
Monitors don't affect ransomware risk.
A warning banner on the login screen
A banner is a weak deterrent and doesn't help recovery.

q.q: An IDS raises an alert and an analyst restores a defaced web page from backup. Which control types were used, in order?
o: Detective, then corrective
Right. The IDS found the problem, and the restore fixed it.
Preventive, then detective
Nothing here prevented the defacement.
Deterrent, then compensating
The IDS didn't discourage the attack, and restoring isn't a substitute control.
Corrective, then preventive
The order is wrong, and a restore is corrective, not preventive.

q.q: Why should every security control have a documented owner?
o: So someone keeps it working and reviews it
Right. Unowned controls drift out of date and nobody notices when they fail.
So auditors know whom to blame
Ownership is about keeping the control working, not blame.
So the control can skip change management reviews
Owned controls still go through change management.
So the control never needs testing
Owners make sure controls are tested.

q.q: A firewall rule was added years ago for a project that ended. No one knows if it's still needed. What is the BEST practice?
o: Review rules with their purpose and owner; remove unneeded ones
Right. Rule reviews with documented purposes stop old openings from piling up.
Leave it in place, because removing any rule can break production traffic
Unneeded rules are open doors. Remove them through change management.
Delete every rule older than one year
Some old rules are still needed. Review them, don't delete them blindly.
Copy the rule to a second firewall as a backup
Copying it spreads the risk.

q.q: During a network scan, the team finds 14 devices that aren't in the asset inventory. What should happen FIRST?
o: Identify each device and its owner
Right. Unknown devices can't be patched or monitored, so they must be identified and handled.
Ignore them, because the scanner might be reporting wrong results
Unknown devices are a common way in for attackers.
Unplug every device on the network
That stops the business. Investigate the unknown ones first.
Buy a new firewall
A firewall doesn't tell you what the devices are.

q.q: Which item belongs in a software asset inventory, not just a hardware one?
o: Each app's version and license
Right. Versions show what needs patching, and licenses show what's allowed.
The serial number and purchase date of each laptop
That's hardware inventory.
The room each server sits in
That's hardware location.
The weight of each switch
Weight isn't a security attribute.

q.q: A team wants to retire a database server. Which step protects the data at END OF LIFE?
o: Sanitize or destroy the drives and record the certificate of destruction
Right. Data must be made unrecoverable, with proof, before hardware leaves.
Delete the database and reuse the drives in a public kiosk
Deleted data can often be recovered.
Unplug the server and leave it in storage
Stored drives still hold the data.
Rename the server so no one recognizes it
Renaming doesn't protect the data.

q.q: Before approving a change that opens a new port on the firewall, what should the change advisory board review FIRST?
o: A security impact analysis of the change
Right. The board needs to know what risk the change adds before it approves it.
The admin's years of experience
Experience doesn't replace analyzing the change.
Whether the change can be done during lunch
Timing matters, but risk comes first.
The color coding on the network diagram
Diagram style isn't part of approval.

q.q: A server's settings no longer match its approved baseline, but no change ticket explains why. What is this called?
o: Configuration drift
Right. Unrecorded changes have moved the system away from its baseline.
A rollback
A rollback restores the previous state on purpose.
Patch management
Patching is a planned change. This is unplanned.
Separation of duties
SoD splits tasks between people.

q.q: An emergency patch must go in tonight to stop an active exploit. What should the change process do?
o: Make an emergency change, then document and review it
Right. Emergency procedures let urgent fixes happen while keeping a record and a later review.
Wait for next week's change board meeting to approve it properly
Waiting leaves the system open to an active attack.
Install it with no record at all
Every change should be recorded, even emergencies.
Turn off change management permanently
One emergency doesn't justify losing control of changes.

q.q: Which training plan is MOST effective for developers?
o: Hands-on secure coding training for their own stack
Right. Training that matches the job and tools changes how people actually work.
The same 10-minute video everyone in the company watches
General awareness doesn't teach secure coding.
A poster in the break room about strong passwords
A poster doesn't cover developer risks.
A yearly quiz with no follow-up
One quiz without feedback changes little.

q.q: The security team runs a tabletop exercise for executives on a ransomware attack. Which goal fits this exercise BEST?
o: Let leaders rehearse decisions, like whether to pay
Right. Tabletops rehearse roles and decisions without touching systems.
Test whether last month's backup tapes can actually be read and restored
That needs a hands-on restore test.
Find unpatched servers
That's a vulnerability scan.
Measure network speed
Exercises don't measure bandwidth.

q.q: A data center visitor log shows several people entered on one badge swipe. Which physical control would BEST stop this?
o: An access control vestibule (mantrap)
Right. A vestibule stops tailgating and piggybacking.
A brighter light over the door
Lighting helps cameras but doesn't stop someone following through.
A sign at the door asking everyone not to let others follow them in
A sign is a weak deterrent.
A longer badge PIN
The problem is extra people walking in, not the badge PIN.

q.q: Why should a security practitioner review badge reader logs alongside VPN and login logs?
o: To spot conflicts, like a badge-in during a foreign login
Right. Physical and logical logs together reveal stolen credentials or shared badges.
Because badge logs replace login logs, so the SIEM can drop the login data
They show different things, so you need both.
To find out who parks closest to the door
Parking isn't a security signal here.
Because badge systems can't be hacked
Badge systems can be attacked too.

q.q: Which pair is TRUE multifactor authentication?
o: A smart card and its PIN
Right. Something you have plus something you know are two different factors.
A password and a security question
Both are something you know, so it's still one factor.
A fingerprint and a face scan
Both are something you are.
Two different passwords
Two of the same factor type isn't MFA.

q.q: A company's users approve push notifications for MFA, and attackers are now flooding users with prompts until someone taps Approve. Which change BEST stops this?
o: Number matching on each push prompt
Right. The user can only approve a login they're actually looking at, which defeats MFA fatigue.
Sending more push prompts so users get used to them
That makes the fatigue attack easier.
Switching everyone to SMS codes, which can't be flooded the same way
SMS is weaker and open to SIM swapping.
Removing MFA for users who complain
That removes the protection completely.

q.q: A user logs in once to the company portal and can then open the HR app, email and the wiki without logging in again. What makes this possible?
o: Single sign-on (SSO)
Right. One authentication event gives access to many trusted apps.
Multifactor authentication
MFA is about how many factors, not how many apps.
Mandatory access control
MAC is an authorization model, not a login method.
Port security
Port security limits devices on a switch port.

q.q: A partner company's employees need to log in to your supplier portal using their own company accounts. What lets your portal trust their logins?
o: Federation using a standard like SAML or OpenID Connect
Right. Federation lets one organization accept another's authentication.
Creating local portal accounts with shared passwords
Shared passwords break accountability and are hard to remove.
Giving the partner your domain admin password
That hands over full control of your domain.
Turning off authentication for partners
That lets anyone in.

q.q: Which authentication method resists phishing BEST?
o: A FIDO2 security key or passkey
Right. The key checks the site's real address, so it won't sign in to a fake site.
A one-time code sent by SMS
Users can be tricked into typing the code into a fake site.
A 6-digit code from an authenticator app
Those codes can also be phished and replayed quickly.
A long password changed every 30 days
Any password can be typed into a fake site.

q.q: Domain A trusts Domain B, and Domain B trusts Domain C. Under a TRANSITIVE trust, what follows?
o: Domain A also trusts Domain C
Right. Transitive trust passes along the chain.
Domain C trusts Domain A
Trust direction isn't reversed by transitivity.
No domain trusts any other
The stated trusts still exist.
Domain B stops trusting Domain C
Transitivity doesn't remove trusts.

q.q: A company gives a supplier limited access to an order system through a separate network zone. What is this zone called?
o: An extranet
Right. An extranet extends limited, controlled access to outside partners.
An intranet
An intranet is only for internal users.
A honeynet
A honeynet is a decoy network for attackers.
A flat network
A flat network has no separation at all.

q.q: Why is a one-way trust safer than a two-way trust between your network and a vendor's?
o: Only the side that needs access is trusted
Right. Limiting trust direction limits what a compromise on one side can reach.
One-way trusts don't need any authentication from the vendor's users
Users still authenticate. Trust just decides whose logins are accepted.
One-way trusts are faster
Speed isn't the security benefit.
One-way trusts encrypt all traffic
Trust direction has nothing to do with encryption.

q.q: A third-party managed service provider (MSP) needs remote admin access to your servers. Which control matters MOST?
o: Named MSP accounts with MFA, least privilege and logging
Right. Third-party access must be accountable, limited and monitored, since MSPs are a common attack path.
One shared admin account for the whole MSP team, with a strong password
Shared accounts break accountability.
A trust that never expires so the MSP isn't locked out
Access should be reviewed and ended when the contract ends.
Letting the MSP install any tool it likes
Unreviewed tools can bring malware or backdoors.

q.q: Before creating an account for a new remote hire, HR confirms her government ID and employment paperwork. Which step is this?
o: Identity proofing
Right. Proofing confirms the person is who they claim to be before an identity is created.
Deprovisioning
Deprovisioning removes access.
Authorization
Authorization decides what she can do after she logs in.
Accounting
Accounting logs what she does.

q.q: A quarterly access review finds that a manager approved access he didn't understand for 40 people. How can the review be made MORE effective?
o: Explain each permission and flag unusual access
Right. Reviewers can only catch excess access if they understand what they're approving.
Have reviewers approve everything at once to save time during busy quarters
Rubber-stamp reviews catch nothing.
Do reviews every five years
Less often means more privilege creep.
Let each user review their own access
Self-review has an obvious conflict of interest.

q.q: An employee's account shows access to six systems her role never needed, picked up through several job changes. What is this called?
o: Privilege creep
Right. Access piles up when old rights aren't removed during role changes.
Least privilege
Least privilege is the goal she's drifted away from.
Federation
Federation is trust between organizations.
Password spraying
Password spraying is an attack technique.

q.q: Which system automates provisioning, deprovisioning and access reviews from HR events?
o: An IGA system
Right. IGA connects HR events to account changes and runs reviews.
A SIEM
A SIEM collects and correlates logs.
A web application firewall in front of the HR portal
A WAF filters web traffic.
A DLP system
DLP watches for sensitive data leaving.

q.q: A cloud app allows access only if the user is in Finance, using a company-managed device, from the U.S., during business hours. Which model is this?
o: Attribute-based access control (ABAC)
Right. The decision uses attributes of the user, device, location and time.
Discretionary access control (DAC)
The file owner isn't deciding here.
Role-based access control (RBAC)
RBAC uses the role alone, not device, place or time.
Mandatory access control (MAC)
MAC uses classification labels and clearances.

q.q: Which model is the BEST fit for a large company where people change jobs often and access should follow the job?
o: Role-based access control (RBAC)
Right. Moving a person to a new role swaps their access in one step.
Discretionary access control (DAC)
With DAC, each owner grants access by hand, which doesn't scale.
Mandatory access control (MAC)
MAC suits classified environments, not frequent job changes.
No access control model
Every organization needs one.

q.q: In a MAC system, a user cleared for Secret tries to save a document to a folder labeled Unclassified, and the system blocks it. Why?
o: Writing down could leak Secret data to a lower label
Right. MAC confidentiality models stop data from flowing to lower labels.
Users cleared for Secret aren't allowed to write any files at all
They can write at their own level or higher, not lower.
The folder is full
Storage space isn't the reason in a MAC scenario.
The user forgot to use MFA
Authentication isn't the issue here. The label is.

q.q: A switch's ACL lets only the management VLAN reach the switch's SSH port. Which access control approach is this?
o: Rule-based access control
Right. A fixed rule applies to all traffic, no matter who the user is.
Discretionary access control
No owner is granting access.
Attribute-based access control
There's only one simple network rule, not policy over many attributes.
Mandatory access control
No classification labels are involved.

q.q: An admin creates a temporary admin role that expires after 2 hours and needs a manager's approval each time. What is this approach called?
o: Just-in-time (JIT) privileged access
Right. Privileges exist only when needed and for a short time.
Standing privilege
Standing privilege is permanent access, which is the opposite.
Single sign-on
SSO is about logging in once.
Role explosion
Role explosion is having too many roles to manage.

q.q: A server is worth $40,000. A flood would destroy 25% of its value, and floods are expected once every 10 years. What is the annualized loss expectancy (ALE)?
o: That's the single loss expectancy, before multiplying by how often it happens.
That uses the wrong numbers. Multiply value by exposure factor, then by the yearly rate.
That multiplies by 10 instead of 0.1. The flood happens once in 10 years.

q.q: Using the ALE from a risk analysis, when is a control worth buying?
o: When it costs less per year than the loss it prevents
Right. A control should cost less than the risk it removes.
Whenever a vendor recommends it
Vendor advice isn't a cost-benefit analysis.
Only when it costs more than the asset, to show the risk is taken seriously
Spending more than the asset's worth makes no sense.
Never, because ALE is only a guess
ALE is an estimate, but it still guides spending decisions.

q.q: Which NIST framework walks an organization through categorizing a system, selecting controls, implementing, assessing, authorizing and monitoring them?
o: The NIST Risk Management Framework (RMF)
Right. Those are the RMF's steps for managing system risk.
The NIST Privacy Framework
That framework focuses on privacy risk.
The OSI model
OSI describes network layers.
The Cyber Kill Chain
The Kill Chain describes attacker stages.

q.q: A company decides it won't launch a new mobile payment feature because the fraud risk is too high. Which risk treatment is this?
o: Avoidance
Right. Not doing the risky activity removes the risk.
Mitigation
Mitigation would add controls and still launch.
Transference
Nothing was shifted to another party.
Acceptance
Accepting would mean launching and living with the risk.

q.q: A U.S. company stores data about customers in France. Which law MOST likely applies to that personal data even though the company is in the U.S.?
o: The EU's GDPR
Right. GDPR covers personal data of people in the EU, wherever the company is.
HIPAA
HIPAA covers U.S. health information.
SOX
SOX covers financial reporting by public companies.
FERPA
FERPA covers U.S. student education records.

q.q: A security analyst wants to read a coworker's personal email account to investigate a possible leak. What should she do FIRST?
o: Check with legal and HR first
Right. Monitoring must follow law and policy, and personal accounts are usually off-limits.
Guess the coworker's password and log in quietly to check
That's unauthorized access and likely illegal.
Ask the coworker's friends for the password
That's still unauthorized access.
Post her suspicion in the team chat
That's unfair to the coworker and could damage the investigation.

q.q: A cloud provider stores a company's backups in another country, where local law could let authorities demand the data. Which concern is this?
o: Jurisdiction and data sovereignty
Right. The laws of the country where data sits can apply to it.
Availability of the backup network
Network speed doesn't decide which laws apply.
Key length of the encryption
Encryption strength is a separate issue.
Separation of duties
SoD is about splitting tasks.

q.q: A vulnerability scan reports 300 findings. Which approach ranks them BEST for fixing?
o: Severity, exploitability, exposure and asset value together
Right. Real risk combines severity, exploitability, exposure and asset value.
Fix them alphabetically by CVE number
CVE order has nothing to do with risk.
Fix the easiest ones first, whatever their risk, to cut the count quickly
Quick wins help, but high-risk exposed issues come first.
Fix only the ones with the longest descriptions
Description length isn't a risk measure.

q.q: A scan finds a missing patch, the patch is installed, and then the system is scanned again. Why rescan?
o: To verify the fix worked and close the finding
Right. Verification is the last step of the vulnerability lifecycle.
Because scanners need to warm up
Scanners don't need a warm-up.
To find out who installed the patch
Change records show that, not scans.
To lower the system's CVSS score permanently
CVSS scores describe vulnerabilities, not systems.

q.q: Why do credentialed (authenticated) vulnerability scans usually find MORE than uncredentialed scans?
o: They log in and check from the inside
Right. Logging in lets the scanner see patch levels and configs it can't see from the network.
They're allowed to exploit every vulnerability they find to confirm it
Scans identify issues. They don't exploit them.
They scan more IP addresses
Scope is set separately from credentials.
They turn off the target's firewall
Scanners shouldn't change the target's settings.

q.q: A scan flags a vulnerability on a server, but the vulnerable service turns out to be disabled. What is this?
o: A false positive
Right. The scanner reported a problem that isn't actually exploitable.
A false negative
A false negative is a real problem the scanner missed.
A zero-day
A zero-day has no patch yet. This one isn't even active.
A true positive
It would be a true positive only if the service were really vulnerable.

q.q: A SIEM is missing logs from the domain controllers. Why is this a serious gap?
o: They record logins and account changes
Right. Authentication logs are among the most valuable sources for detection.
Domain controllers only log printer jobs and DHCP leases
They log authentication and directory changes.
SIEMs can't read Windows logs
SIEMs commonly ingest Windows event logs.
It isn't a gap, because firewalls log everything
Firewalls don't see who logged in or what changed in the directory.

q.q: Two servers' log times are 7 minutes apart, which makes correlating an attack confusing. What fixes this?
o: Sync every device to a trusted NTP time source
Right. Consistent timestamps let events from different systems line up.
Turn off timestamps
Without timestamps you can't build a timeline at all.
Store logs on the same server they come from
Storage location doesn't fix clock drift.
Rotate logs more often
Rotation doesn't fix wrong times.

q.q: Why should logs be sent to a central server that attackers on a host can't easily change?
o: Attackers often wipe a host's local logs
Right. Central, protected logs survive even if the host is compromised.
Central servers make logs smaller
Size isn't the main reason.
Local logs are always encrypted
Local logs can be read and changed by an admin-level attacker.
Central logging removes the need for any log retention rules
You still need retention rules.

q.q: A team adds an AI-based anomaly detector to its monitoring platform. What should it do BEFORE trusting the detector's alerts?
o: Baseline normal behavior and tune it
Right. Anomaly detection only works once it knows what normal looks like.
Turn off all signature-based detection
Signatures still catch known threats.
Send every alert straight to leadership so nothing gets missed
Untuned alerts will be noisy.
Give the detector admin rights on every server
Monitoring tools need read access to data, not admin rights everywhere.

q.q: A file server usually sends about 2 GB a day to the internet. Last night it sent 60 GB to an unknown host. What should the analyst do FIRST?
o: Investigate it as possible exfiltration
Right. A big jump from the baseline to an unknown host is a classic exfiltration sign.
Ignore it, since file servers send data out to backup services all the time
The amount and destination are far outside normal.
Delete the file server's logs to save space
That destroys evidence.
Order a faster internet connection
Bandwidth isn't the issue.

q.q: Failed logins for one account went from 3 a day to 3,000 in an hour, from many IP addresses. What does this pattern suggest?
o: A brute-force or password-spraying attack
Right. A sudden flood of failures from many sources points to automated guessing.
The user forgot their password
One person forgetting wouldn't cause thousands of failures from many IPs.
A normal patch cycle
Patching doesn't cause failed logins.
A DNS outage
DNS problems don't create login failures.

q.q: After analyzing an alert, the analyst finds it was a real attack that was blocked. What should she do with the finding?
o: Document the evidence and outcome, and report it
Right. Documenting and reporting turns monitoring into lessons and metrics.
Close it with no notes, since the attack was blocked and nothing was lost
Blocked attacks still show who's targeting you and how.
Delete the alert so the dashboard looks clean
That hides useful information.
Email the attacker to warn them
Never contact attackers.

q.q: In NIST's incident response life cycle, which phase includes writing playbooks, setting up contact lists and training the team?
o: Preparation
Right. Preparation gets people, tools and plans ready before an incident.
Containment, eradication and recovery
That phase handles an incident already happening.
Detection and analysis
That phase finds and confirms incidents.
Post-incident activity
That phase reviews an incident after it's over.

q.q: An analyst sees ransomware encrypting files on a file server. Which action comes FIRST?
o: Isolate the server from the network
Right. Containment limits damage before eradication and recovery.
Pay the ransom right away
Paying is a leadership decision and doesn't stop the spread.
Restore the server from last night's backup immediately
Restoring before containment can reinfect the system.
Write the lessons-learned report
That comes at the end.

q.q: A level-1 analyst confirms that an alert involves a domain admin account. The playbook says privileged account incidents go to the incident manager. What is this step?
o: Escalation
Right. Serious incidents are passed to higher authority as the playbook defines.
Eradication
Eradication removes the threat.
Recovery
Recovery restores normal operations.
Accounting
Accounting is logging what users do.

q.q: After removing malware, the team rebuilds the server from a clean image and watches it closely for a week. Which phase is this?
o: Recovery
Right. Recovery returns systems to service and confirms they're clean.
Preparation
Preparation happens before incidents.
Detection
Detection was earlier.
Containment
Containment came before the rebuild.

q.q: Why should incident playbooks be written for common scenarios like phishing and ransomware?
o: They give tested steps for fast, consistent action
Right. Playbooks cut decision time and mistakes during an incident.
They replace the need for trained staff during an incident
Playbooks guide people. They don't replace them.
They're only needed for audits
Their main value is during real incidents.
They make incidents less likely to happen
Playbooks improve response, not likelihood.

q.q: Which evidence should a responder collect FIRST from a running, compromised server?
o: Memory (RAM)
Right. Collect the most volatile evidence first.
The hard drive image
The disk keeps its data after power-off, so it can wait.
Printed copies of the server manual
Manuals aren't evidence.
Backup tapes from last year, kept in the offsite vault
Old backups don't change. Volatile data does.

q.q: A responder hashes a disk image right after making it, then hashes it again before analysis. Why?
o: To prove the image hasn't changed
Right. Matching hashes show integrity, which matters in court.
To encrypt the image
Hashing doesn't encrypt.
To make the image smaller
Hashing doesn't compress the data.
To speed up the analysis tools when they index the image
Hashes are for integrity, not speed.

q.q: A detective asks to borrow a hard drive from an investigation for a day. What must happen?
o: Record the handoff on the custody form
Right. Every transfer of evidence must be recorded.
Hand it over without paperwork, since he's police
Even police transfers must be recorded.
Make a copy and give him the original without noting it
Any handling of the original must be documented.
Refuse, because evidence can never leave the room
It can be transferred if custody is recorded.

q.q: Why should analysts examine a forensic COPY of a drive instead of the original?
o: Analysis could alter the original evidence
Right. Working on a verified copy protects the original's integrity.
Copies are faster to read
Speed isn't the main reason.
Originals can't be read by forensic tools without special licenses
Tools can read them, but you shouldn't risk changing them.
Copies don't need a chain of custody
Copies are documented too.

q.q: An investigation might end up in court. What should the final forensic report include?
o: The facts, plus the method and tools used
Right. A repeatable, factual method makes findings trustworthy.
The analyst's guesses about who is to blame, to help the lawyers
Reports stick to evidence, not speculation.
Only the conclusion, with no method
Without the method, others can't check the work.
Personal opinions about the suspect's character
That isn't evidence.

q.q: A company needs its critical systems running within minutes of a disaster and is willing to pay a lot for it. Which alternate site fits?
o: A hot site
Right. A hot site is fully equipped with current data and can take over almost at once.
A cold site
A cold site has space and power but no equipment ready. Recovery takes weeks.
A warm site
A warm site has some equipment but needs hours or days to be ready.
A reciprocal agreement with a competitor
These are hard to rely on and rarely ready in minutes.

q.q: After a disaster, which systems should be restored FIRST?
o: The most critical ones, as ranked in the BIA
Right. The business impact analysis decides restoration order.
The systems that are easiest and quickest to restore from backup
Easy isn't the same as important.
The CEO's personal laptop
Executive devices aren't automatically the most critical.
Whatever the vendor suggests
The organization's BIA decides priorities.

q.q: A company copies its data to a second data center as each change happens. Which goal does this mainly support?
o: A very low recovery point objective (RPO)
Right. Real-time replication means almost no data is lost.
A lower electricity bill
Replication uses more resources, not less.
Stronger passwords
Replication doesn't affect passwords.
Separation of duties
SoD isn't related to data copies.

q.q: Ransomware also encrypted the company's online backups. Which backup practice would have prevented this?
o: An offline or immutable backup copy
Right. Backups the attacker can't reach or modify survive ransomware.
Backing up more often to the same online share
More copies in the same reachable place get encrypted too.
Using bigger backup drives
Size doesn't stop encryption.
Renaming the backup folder
Ransomware doesn't care about folder names.

q.q: The DR team fails over to the backup data center for a real weekend test, then fails back. Which test is this?
o: A full-interruption test
Right. Production actually moves to the recovery site.
A tabletop exercise
Tabletops are discussions only.
A checklist review
That's reading the plan, not running it.
A walk-through
A walk-through steps through the plan without failing over.

q.q: What is the role of an emergency response plan during a fire at the data center?
o: Protect people first: evacuate and account for staff
Right. Life safety always comes before systems.
Save the servers before anyone leaves
People come before equipment.
Restart the servers at the backup site before evacuating anyone from the building
Evacuate first. Recovery comes later.
Send a press release
Communication comes after people are safe.

q.q: A company runs two web servers behind a load balancer so one can fail without an outage. What is this?
o: Redundancy (high availability)
Right. Extra capacity keeps the service up when one part fails.
A cold site
A cold site is a separate recovery location.
Data masking
Masking hides data.
Mandatory access control
MAC is an access model.

q.q: A regulation says stored customer data must be unreadable if a laptop is stolen. Which requirement drives the encryption choice?
o: Confidentiality of data at rest
Right. Full-disk encryption keeps stored data unreadable without the key.
Integrity of data in transit
The laptop's stored data is the concern, not network traffic.
Availability of the laptop
Encryption doesn't keep the laptop running.
Non-repudiation of emails
Emails and signatures aren't the issue here.

q.q: Why do cryptographic keys need a good source of randomness (entropy)?
o: Predictable keys can be guessed
Right. A weak random source makes keys easy to recreate.
Random keys make encryption faster
Randomness affects security, not speed.
Entropy makes keys shorter
Key length is chosen separately.
Random keys never need to be rotated or replaced later
Keys still need rotation.

q.q: A message must be proven to come from the sender AND to be unchanged. Which crypto service does this?
o: A digital signature
Right. Signatures give authenticity, integrity and non-repudiation.
Symmetric encryption alone
A shared key can't prove which of the two parties sent it.
Base64 encoding
Encoding isn't encryption or proof of anything.
Compression
Compression doesn't prove origin.

q.q: Two users pick the same password, but their stored hashes are different. What explains this?
o: Each password got its own random salt
Right. Salts make identical passwords hash differently and defeat rainbow tables.
The system encrypts passwords with each user's public key
Passwords should be hashed, not encrypted.
The hash algorithm is random
Hash functions always give the same output for the same input.
One user's password is stored in plain text
Plain text would be a serious flaw, not an explanation.

q.q: Which algorithm is asymmetric?
o: Elliptic curve cryptography (ECC)
Right. ECC uses a public and private key pair.
AES
AES is symmetric.
3DES
3DES is symmetric.
SHA-256
SHA-256 is a hash, not encryption.

q.q: An attacker tries every possible key until one decrypts the message. Which attack is this?
o: A brute-force attack
Right. Brute force tries every possibility, so longer keys defeat it.
A birthday attack
A birthday attack looks for two inputs with the same hash.
A replay attack
A replay resends captured traffic.
A side-channel attack
Side-channel attacks use clues like timing or power use.

q.q: Alice sends Bob a file encrypted with Bob's public key. Who can decrypt it?
o: Only Bob, with his private key
Right. Data encrypted with a public key opens only with the matching private key.
Anyone with Bob's public key
The public key encrypts. It can't decrypt.
Only Alice, with her private key
Alice's key wasn't used.
Anyone who knows the file name
The file name doesn't unlock anything.

q.q: A team still moves files with FTP. Which protocol should replace it?
o: SFTP
Right. SFTP runs over SSH and encrypts logins and data.
TFTP
TFTP has no authentication or encryption.
Telnet
Telnet is a clear-text remote shell.
HTTP
HTTP isn't encrypted.

q.q: Two branch offices need an always-on encrypted link over the internet between their routers. Which protocol fits BEST?
o: IPsec in tunnel mode
Right. IPsec tunnels encrypt everything between the two sites.
SNMPv1
SNMPv1 is for monitoring and isn't encrypted.
SMTP
SMTP moves email.
Plain HTTP
HTTP isn't encrypted.

q.q: A web server still allows TLS 1.0 and old ciphers. What is the BEST fix?
o: Allow only TLS 1.2 and 1.3
Right. Retiring old versions removes known weaknesses.
Switch the site to plain HTTP
That removes encryption completely.
Turn off the certificate
The site needs its certificate for HTTPS.
Allow every TLS version so older clients stay compatible
Old versions keep the site exposed.

q.q: An employee's laptop, which held her signing certificate's private key, is stolen. What should happen to the certificate?
o: Revoke it through the CA
Right. Revocation tells everyone to stop trusting the stolen key.
Let it expire on its own
It could be misused until it expires.
Email everyone a copy of the private key
That spreads the compromised key.
Renew it with the same key pair so nothing breaks
The key pair is compromised and must be replaced.

q.q: A browser trusts a website's certificate. What does that trust come from?
o: It chains to a root CA the browser trusts
Right. PKI trust flows from trusted root CAs through intermediates.
The website's logo
Logos are easy to copy.
The website's fast loading
Speed isn't trust.
The certificate being self-signed by the site's own server
Browsers don't trust self-signed certificates by default.

q.q: Where should a certificate authority keep its root private key?
o: Offline, in a hardware security module
Right. If the root key is stolen, every certificate under it becomes untrusted.
On a public web server so anyone can verify it
The public certificate is shared. The private key never is.
In an email folder for easy recovery
Email is far too exposed for a root key.
On every employee's laptop
Spreading the key makes theft likely.

q.q: Which TCP/IP model layer lines up with OSI layers 5, 6 and 7?
o: The Application layer
Right. TCP/IP's Application layer covers OSI's Session, Presentation and Application layers.
The Transport layer
Transport matches OSI layer 4.
The Internet layer
Internet matches OSI layer 3.
The Network Access layer
Network Access matches OSI layers 1 and 2.

q.q: In a software-defined network (SDN), what does the controller do?
o: It centrally decides how traffic flows
Right. SDN separates the control plane (decisions) from the data plane (forwarding).
It replaces every cable in the network
SDN still uses physical links.
It encrypts all traffic automatically
SDN is about control, not built-in encryption.
It only stores nightly backups of every switch config
That's configuration backup, not SDN control.

q.q: An analyst sees outbound traffic to TCP 3389 from a workstation to an internet host. Which service is this?
o: Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP)
Right. TCP 3389 is RDP, which shouldn't usually go out to the internet.
DNS
DNS uses port 53.
LDAPS
LDAPS uses port 636.
Syslog
Syslog uses port 514.

q.q: A web shop is overwhelmed by traffic from thousands of hacked home devices. Which countermeasure helps MOST?
o: A DDoS protection service or CDN
Right. Large distributed attacks need capacity and filtering upstream of your site.
A stronger admin password
Passwords don't stop traffic floods.
Full-disk encryption on the web server and database
Encryption doesn't absorb traffic.
Blocking one IP address
The attack comes from thousands of addresses.

q.q: Users on the guest Wi-Fi are sent to a fake bank site when they type the real bank's address. The DNS server has been fed false records. What is this attack?
o: DNS cache poisoning
Right. False records in the resolver's cache send users to the attacker.
SQL injection
SQL injection targets databases through input fields.
ARP flooding
That overloads a switch's MAC table.
Bluejacking
Bluejacking sends unwanted Bluetooth messages.

q.q: An attacker on the same coffee-shop Wi-Fi intercepts and changes traffic between a user and a site. What is this?
o: An on-path (man-in-the-middle) attack
Right. The attacker sits between the two sides and can read or change traffic.
A denial-of-service attack
DoS stops the service. This attack reads and changes traffic.
Privilege escalation
Escalation means gaining higher rights on a system.
A logic bomb
A logic bomb is code that triggers later.

q.q: A company wants every device to authenticate before a switch port lets it onto the network. Which standard does this?
o: IEEE 802.1X
Right. 802.1X blocks the port until the device or user authenticates, usually through RADIUS.
That's a Wi-Fi speed standard.
Spanning Tree Protocol
STP prevents switching loops.
DHCP
DHCP hands out IP addresses. It doesn't authenticate.

q.q: Network admins want every command they run on routers to be authorized and logged separately. Which AAA protocol fits BEST?
o: TACACS+
Right. TACACS+ separates authentication, authorization and accounting, so each command can be checked and logged.
RADIUS
RADIUS combines authentication and authorization and is mainly for network access.
SNMPv1
SNMP is for monitoring, not admin logins.
Telnet
Telnet is an insecure remote shell, not an AAA protocol.

q.q: Contractors need access to one internal app, but the company doesn't want their laptops on the network. Which remote access option fits BEST?
o: A virtual desktop (VDI) where only the screen reaches the contractor
Right. The app and data stay in the data center.
A full-tunnel VPN that puts their laptops on the internal network
That brings unmanaged laptops onto the network.
Opening the app directly to the internet with no login
That exposes the app to everyone.
Emailing them copies of the database
That sends the data out of the company.

q.q: Where should a company place a web server that customers reach from the internet?
o: In a screened subnet (DMZ)
Right. Public services are kept apart from the internal network.
On the same VLAN as the HR database, behind the firewall
A hacked web server would then reach HR data directly.
On the CEO's desktop
Desktops aren't servers and hold sensitive data.
Outside every firewall with no protection
That leaves it fully exposed.

q.q: Network devices are managed over the same network that users browse the web on. What is the BEST improvement?
o: Use a separate management network
Right. Isolating management traffic keeps admin interfaces away from users and attackers.
Turn off logging on the switches
Logging helps security. Keep it on.
Use Telnet so management is faster
Telnet is clear text and unsafe.
Give every user the switch passwords so they can report problems
That makes the problem worse.

q.q: Why change the default SNMP community strings and move to SNMPv3?
o: Default strings are guessable; v3 adds auth and encryption
Right. SNMPv3 fixes the weak security of older versions.
SNMPv3 makes the switches run faster and use less memory
The change is for security, not speed.
Default strings are required by law
No law requires default strings.
SNMP is used only for printing
SNMP monitors all kinds of devices.

q.q: A company wants to stop employees from emailing spreadsheets that contain Social Security numbers to outside addresses. Which tool fits BEST?
o: Data loss prevention (DLP)
Right. DLP inspects outgoing content for sensitive data patterns and blocks it.
A load balancer
A load balancer spreads traffic across servers.
A NAT router
NAT rewrites addresses. It doesn't inspect content.
A KVM switch
A KVM switch shares a keyboard and monitor between computers.

q.q: What is the main difference between an IDS and an IPS?
o: An IPS can block; an IDS only alerts
Right. Inline placement lets an IPS stop what it detects.
An IDS encrypts the traffic it watches, and an IPS doesn't
Neither one is for encryption.
An IPS only works on wireless networks
IPS works on any network.
They're the same device with different names
They differ in placement and action.

q.q: A forward proxy sits between users and the internet. Which security benefit does it provide?
o: It filters and logs web requests
Right. Proxies enforce browsing rules and give visibility.
It replaces endpoint antivirus
Endpoint protection is still needed.
It stops all phishing emails
A web proxy doesn't handle email.
It makes users anonymous to the security team
It gives the security team more visibility, not less.

q.q: A company wants each employee to log in to Wi-Fi with their own account rather than a shared password. Which setup fits?
o: WPA3-Enterprise using 802.1X with EAP
Right. Enterprise mode authenticates each user, often against the directory through RADIUS.
WPA3-Personal with one shared passphrase
Personal mode uses a shared key.
WEP with a long key
WEP is broken.
An open network with a captive portal only
An open network doesn't encrypt traffic.

q.q: An attacker sets up an access point with the same name as the company's Wi-Fi to trick users into connecting. What is this?
o: An evil twin
Right. A fake access point copies a real SSID to capture users and traffic.
Bluesnarfing
Bluesnarfing steals data over Bluetooth.
War driving
War driving is searching for Wi-Fi networks.
A jamming attack
Jamming blocks the signal instead of copying it.

q.q: Why should employees turn off Bluetooth and NFC on phones when they aren't using them?
o: It shrinks the attack surface
Right. Turning off radios you don't need removes ways in.
It makes Wi-Fi faster
Bluetooth doesn't slow Wi-Fi in a meaningful way.
It's needed to keep the phone's warranty valid
Warranties don't depend on this.
It stops all phishing emails
Radios have nothing to do with email phishing.

q.q: A building has 300 smart sensors whose vendor no longer releases firmware updates. What is the BEST approach?
o: Isolate, monitor and plan to replace them
Right. End-of-life IoT can't be patched, so contain the risk and retire it.
Connect them to the main office network so they're easier to manage
That gives a hacked sensor a path to everything.
Ignore them, since sensors don't hold data
Hacked IoT devices are used to attack other systems.
Give them public IP addresses
That exposes them directly to the internet.

q.q: Which step should come FIRST when installing new IoT cameras?
o: Change defaults and update firmware
Right. Default passwords and old firmware are the most common IoT weaknesses.
Open the cameras to the internet for remote viewing
Exposing them before hardening invites attack.
Disable all logging on the cameras
Logging helps you spot misuse.
Share the admin password with every employee
That removes access control.

q.q: Malware spreads from computer to computer across the network on its own, with no user clicking anything. What type is it?
o: A worm
Right. Worms self-replicate across networks without user action.
A virus
A virus needs a host file and usually a user action to spread.
A Trojan
A Trojan pretends to be useful software and doesn't spread by itself.
Adware
Adware shows unwanted ads.

q.q: A user's files suddenly can't be opened and a note demands payment in cryptocurrency. What should the user do FIRST?
o: Disconnect and report it
Right. Quick isolation and reporting limit the spread.
Pay the ransom from their own account
Paying is an organizational decision and doesn't guarantee recovery.
Restart the computer repeatedly until the files come back
Restarting doesn't decrypt files and can destroy evidence.
Email the note to all coworkers as a warning
The security team should handle communications.

q.q: A database admin starts downloading large amounts of customer data at 2 a.m., which he has never done before. What kind of tool would flag this?
o: User and entity behavior analytics (UEBA)
Right. UEBA learns normal behavior and flags unusual activity, including insiders.
A port scanner
Port scanners find open ports, not unusual user behavior.
A spam filter
Spam filters handle email.
A load balancer
Load balancers spread traffic.

q.q: Malware hides deep in the operating system and lies to antivirus tools about what's running. What type is it?
o: A rootkit
Right. Rootkits hide themselves and other malware by changing how the OS reports activity.
Spyware
Spyware collects information, but hiding at OS level is the rootkit's job.
A logic bomb
A logic bomb triggers on a condition.
Ransomware
Ransomware encrypts files for payment.

q.q: Only approved programs should run on kiosk PCs. Which control enforces this?
o: Application allow listing
Right. Anything not on the approved list is blocked from running.
A host-based firewall
A firewall controls network traffic, not which programs run.
Full-disk encryption
Encryption protects data if the disk is stolen.
A screen saver password
That locks the screen but doesn't control programs.

q.q: What does a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) provide on a laptop?
o: Secure key storage and trusted boot
Right. The TPM protects keys, such as disk encryption keys, and checks boot integrity.
Faster Wi-Fi
The TPM has nothing to do with networking speed.
A backup power supply
That's a battery or UPS.
Built-in antivirus scanning of every file at boot
The TPM doesn't scan for malware.

q.q: EDR flags a laptop running a script that is encrypting files. What EDR feature helps MOST right away?
o: Network isolation of the host
Right. Network isolation stops the spread but keeps the device available for investigation.
Deleting the EDR agent
That removes visibility.
Turning off the laptop's screen
That doesn't stop the script.
Sending the user an automatic reminder about strong passwords
This isn't a password problem.

q.q: Why add a host-based firewall when there's already a network firewall?
o: It protects the device wherever it is
Right. Host firewalls add defense in depth wherever the device goes.
It replaces the network firewall for that device's traffic
Both layers are useful.
It speeds up the internet connection
Firewalls don't add speed.
It encrypts the hard drive
That's disk encryption.

q.q: A company lets staff use personal phones for work email but needs to wipe only company data if a phone is lost. Which feature makes this possible?
o: Containerization of work apps and data
Right. The company can wipe the work container without touching personal photos.
A full factory reset
That erases the employee's personal data too.
A stronger Wi-Fi password at the office and on the guest network
Wi-Fi doesn't separate data on the phone.
Turning off the phone's camera
That doesn't separate or protect data.

q.q: The company buys phones and owns them, but lets employees use them for personal things too. Which provisioning model is this?
o: Corporate-owned, personally enabled (COPE)
Right. The company owns and manages the device and allows personal use.
Bring your own device (BYOD)
In BYOD the employee owns the phone.
Choose your own device (CYOD)
CYOD lets employees pick from a list. Ownership and personal use are separate questions.
Virtual desktop infrastructure (VDI)
VDI is about remote desktops, not phone ownership.

q.q: Which mobile device management (MDM) setting BEST protects company data if a phone is stolen?
o: Required encryption and remote wipe
Right. Encryption protects the data, and remote wipe removes it.
A custom wallpaper with the company logo
Wallpaper doesn't protect anything.
Turning off automatic updates so settings don't change
Updates fix vulnerabilities, so keep them on.
Allowing apps from any source
Unknown app sources increase risk.

q.q: A company wants to control only its own apps on employees' personal phones, without managing the whole device. Which approach fits?
o: Mobile application management (MAM)
Right. MAM manages and protects specific apps and their data.
Full mobile device management of every personal setting
Employees often refuse full control of personal phones.
Disabling the phones' cellular radios
That breaks the phones.
Port security on the office switch
Switch settings don't manage phone apps.

q.q: A company uses PaaS to host an app. Under shared responsibility, who patches the operating system under the app?
o: The cloud provider
Right. In PaaS the provider manages the OS and runtime. The customer manages the app and its data.
The customer
In IaaS the customer would. In PaaS the provider does.
The customer's internet provider
The ISP has no role in the cloud platform.
Nobody, because PaaS has no operating system
There is an OS. The provider manages it.

q.q: Before moving regulated data to a cloud provider, what should the company check about the provider?
o: Its audit reports, like SOC 2, and the contract terms
Right. Third-party assurance and contract terms show whether the provider can meet the company's duties.
Only the price per gigabyte and the length of the free trial
Price alone ignores security and legal duties.
The color of its logo
Branding isn't assurance.
Whether the CEO likes the sales rep
Personal impressions aren't due diligence.

q.q: A company keeps sensitive workloads in its own data center and bursts extra demand to a public cloud. Which deployment model is this?
o: Hybrid cloud
Right. Hybrid combines private and public resources.
Community cloud
Community clouds are shared by organizations with common needs.
Public cloud only
Part of the workload stays private.
Private cloud only
Part of the workload goes to public cloud.

q.q: An attacker breaks out of a virtual machine and gains access to the hypervisor. What is this called?
o: VM escape
Right. Escaping the guest reaches the host and potentially every other VM.
VM sprawl
Sprawl is having too many unmanaged VMs.
Live migration
Live migration moves a running VM between hosts on purpose.
Snapshotting
A snapshot saves a VM's state.

q.q: Which hypervisor runs directly on the server hardware with no host operating system underneath?
o: Type 1 (bare metal)
Right. Type 1 has a smaller attack surface because there's no general-purpose host OS.
Type 2 (hosted)
Type 2 runs as an app on a regular operating system.
A container runtime
Containers share the host OS kernel. They aren't hypervisors.
A web browser
Browsers aren't hypervisors.

q.q: How do containers differ from virtual machines in a way that affects security?
o: Containers share the host's kernel
Right. Lighter isolation means the shared kernel must be kept patched and hardened.
Containers each have their own full operating system
That describes VMs.
Containers can't be scanned for vulnerabilities like VMs can
Container images can and should be scanned.
Containers never need patching
Images and hosts need regular patching.

q.q: Dozens of old, unpatched VMs that nobody owns are still running in a cluster. Which problem is this, and what fixes it?
o: VM sprawl; give VMs owners or retire them
Right. Untracked VMs aren't patched or monitored, so they need owners or removal.
VM escape; turn off the hypervisor until every VM is patched
This isn't an escape, and turning off the hypervisor stops everything.
Data masking; mask the VM names
Renaming hides nothing from attackers.
Federation; trust another company's VMs
Federation is about identity trust.

q.title: Pick the access control model
q.scenario: Five access rules from different systems. Pick the model each one uses.

rows.req: A file's owner shares her folder with two teammates.
rows.why: The owner decides who gets in: discretionary.

rows.req: Users cleared for Secret can read Secret files, and labels can't be changed by users.
Everyone added to the Helpdesk group can reset passwords.
rows.why: Access comes from the job role.

rows.req: No one can log in to the HR app between 10 p.m. and 5 a.m.
Access is allowed only for Finance staff on managed laptops in the U.S.
rows.why: Several attributes of user, device and location together.

q.title: Choose the recovery setup
q.scenario: Five systems need a recovery plan. Pick the alternate site type that best fits each one's recovery time and budget.

rows.req: Online payments. Must be back within 15 minutes; money is no issue.
rows.why: Only a hot site, already running with current data, can take over in minutes.

rows.req: Archive of old project files. A few weeks without it is fine.
rows.why: A cold site is cheapest and fine when recovery can take weeks.

rows.req: Internal ticketing. Should return within a day or two at moderate cost.
rows.why: A warm site has some equipment ready, so recovery takes hours to days.

rows.req: Call center phone system. Must be back within the hour.
rows.why: An hour is too short for a warm site to be built out.

rows.req: Training lab used twice a year. Cost matters most.
rows.why: Low priority and low budget fit a cold site.

q.title: Put each action in its incident response phase
q.scenario: Actions from a recent incident. Pick the NIST incident response phase each one belongs to. Each phase can be used more than once, and one option is a distractor.

items.text: Writing the phishing playbook and testing the call tree.
items.why: Getting ready before an incident is preparation.

items.text: Confirming that an EDR alert is a real compromise and judging its scope.
items.why: Confirming and sizing an incident is detection and analysis.

items.text: Isolating the infected laptop and blocking the attacker's IP.
Rebuilding the server from a clean image and restoring data.
items.why: Rebuilding and restoring is eradication and recovery.

items.text: Holding a blameless review and updating the playbook.
items.why: Reviewing and improving afterward is post-incident activity.

q.title: Match the tool to the job
q.scenario: Five network problems. Pick the appliance or service that best solves each one. Two options are distractors.

items.text: Stop spreadsheets with customer SSNs from being emailed outside the company.
items.why: DLP inspects outgoing content for sensitive data.

items.text: Block exploit traffic aimed at a web server, inline, as it arrives.
items.why: An IPS sits inline and blocks malicious traffic.

items.text: Filter which websites users can visit and log their browsing.
items.why: A forward proxy filters and logs web requests.

items.text: Keep unpatched laptops off the network until they're compliant.
items.why: NAC checks device health before allowing access.

items.text: Spread customer traffic across three web servers.
items.why: A load balancer distributes traffic for availability.

q.title: Choose the crypto for each need
q.scenario: Five security needs. Pick the cryptographic tool that fits each one best.

rows.req: Encrypt a 200 GB backup quickly with a key both sites already share.
rows.why: Symmetric encryption like AES is fast for large data.

rows.req: Safely exchange a session key with a server you've never talked to.
rows.why: Public key cryptography solves key exchange.

rows.req: Check that a downloaded ISO matches the vendor's published fingerprint.
Store user passwords so identical passwords don't look the same.
rows.why: A unique salt per password defeats rainbow tables.

rows.req: Prove a contract came from the CFO and wasn't changed.
rows.why: A signature gives authenticity, integrity and non-repudiation.
